slides.0.title: Grape Varieties
slides.0.subtitle: Grenache, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Tibouren, and Niellucciu, Sciaccarellu and Vermentinu
slides.1.title: Provence's main red grapes
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The five principal varieties of Côtes de Provence
slides.1.highlights.0.content: INAO specification: the principal varieties for red and rosé are Cinsault, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah and Tibouren; Cabernet Sauvignon, Caladoc, Carignan and others are accessory, and Cabernet Sauvignon is not a principal variety
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Tibouren's local character
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Earthy, garrigue aromas, mostly used for rosé; sensitive to coulure so rarely planted alone; it may come from Greece, though one account says it reached Saint-Tropez only in the 18th century (Wikipedia); in Liguria, Italy it is called Rossese
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Mourvèdre and Bandol
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Mourvèdre must make up 50% to 95% of Bandol red, with top cuvées often at 80–95%, partnered by Grenache and Cinsault (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.content: Provence rosé aromas come mainly from combinations of Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah.
slides.2.title: Provence's white and local grapes
slides.2.highlights.0.title: White varieties
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The principal varieties for Côtes de Provence white are Clairette, Sémillon, Ugni Blanc and Vermentino (INAO); Vermentino is also called Rolle locally (INAO, Bellet)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Bellet's unique grapes
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Bellet's red and rosé rest on Braquet and Fuella nera, with Vermentino for white (INAO specification)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Cassis white
slides.2.highlights.2.content: About 70% of Cassis is white, built on Marsanne and Clairette (Wine With Seth); Wikipedia also lists Ugni Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc
slides.2.content: Rosé leads, but white grapes are the signature of the small coastal appellations.
slides.3.title: Corsica's island varieties
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Niellucciu (Nielluccio)
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Very close to Sangiovese (possibly the same variety or a clone); Patrimonio red needs at least 90% Nielluccio (INAO), while Wine With Seth cites 95%, so INAO is followed; powerful and spicy, nicknamed "the spice wine of France"
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Sciaccarellu (Sciacarello)
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Called Mammolo in Italy and grown mainly around Ajaccio and Sartène; highly aromatic with pepper and spice, light in body with good acidity, making herb-scented reds and pale rosés (Wine With Seth); sources disagree on the Ajaccio minimum (60% or 40%), so it is not tested
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Vermentinu and the others
slides.3.highlights.2.content: White rests on Vermentinu (called malvoisie de Corse by INAO) and Patrimonio white uses Vermentino only; the island has 33 varieties, including Biancu Gentile, Aleaticu, Muscat à petits grains, Barbarossa and Genovese (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.content: Corsica's distinction is its island grapes, not replaced by international varieties.
